title: intention
hookLine: intention; the difference between saying and meaning

lines: HOME, AND NO MEMORY OF THE DRIVE.
cards: Someone drives home and pulls into the driveway without remembering a single turn. Someone reads a whole page, reaches the bottom, and has no idea what it said.
Someone says love you at the end of a phone call the way they'd say bye. The mouth did the job. Nobody was there.
Now imagine a tradition with words it says every day, morning and night, for a lifetime. The danger isn't forgetting them. It's saying them perfectly while you're somewhere else entirely.
Judaism has a word for what's missing. Today: intention.

teach.b: Kavanah comes from a root that means to aim, to direct, to point something at a target. Intention is aiming your heart where your words are going.
The rabbis, discussing the Shema from yesterday, said that if a person directed their heart while reading it, they had done what was asked.
They also remembered that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, just to direct their hearts.
An hour of aiming, for a few minutes of prayer. The Bible's clearest picture of kavanah is a woman named Hannah, praying at the sanctuary for a child.
She speaks in her heart; only her lips move, and no sound comes out. The priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't.
She's praying as hard as anyone ever has, and the rabbis learned much of how to pray from her. One old line puts it simply: the Merciful One wants the heart. Then the honest part.
The rabbis argued about whether a commandment done without intention still counts, and the discussion went on for centuries. Many say yes, the act counts, but it isn't the whole thing.
And one teaching holds both sides together: do the good thing even when your heart isn't in it, because from doing it without the right intention, you come to do it with the right one.

teach.h: THE MERCIFUL ONE WANTS THE HEART.
teach.b: That's day ten again, do first, with a promise attached. This week you met Abraham, Jacob, Sinai, Shabbat, shalom, the Shema, and now the thing that makes any of them more than motions.

how: Jews pray fixed prayers three times a day and try to say them with kavanah; many pause before praying to focus, and the silent standing prayer, the Amidah, is said with moving lips and no sound, as Hannah prayed.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the priest thought Hannah was drunk
her lips moved and no sound came out. she was praying.
the rabbis agreed that a commandment without intention doesn't count
they argued for centuries; many say the act counts but isn't the whole thing.
kavanah means saying the words perfectly
it means aiming your heart where the words are going.

games.q: you're about to do a good deed, but your heart isn't in it today. what does the old teaching say?
o: wait until you really mean it.
do it anyway: the meaning grows from the doing.
games.why: do it: from doing it without the right intention, you come to do it with the right one.

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Pick one short thing you say every day without thinking: thank you, good morning, love you, or, if you pray, the Shema.
For the first part of the sit, just aim: who is it for, and what do you actually mean by it? Then say it once, slowly, meaning every word.

wordCard.voice: Kavanah. Intention: aiming your heart where your words and actions are going. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.

orig.note: Hebrew: intention, from a root meaning to aim or direct.

carryVoice: Your line: mean it. Two weeks in, that's the thread running through all of them. Week two, done.
